To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we developed a novel approach to selectively target complement regulatory proteins to red blood cells, which is an attractive concept for the site-specific inhibition of the complement cascade in disease.
a novel targeting concept was established that allowed for the selective reconstitution of a cell type with a complement regulatory protein.

a recombinant form of complement regulatory protein can be delivered to a defined cell population using a single-chain antibody fragment as a vehicle and that this strategy can be used to correct a complement regulatory protein deficiency in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the in vivo application of complement regulatory proteins and the development of novel therapeutic approaches in the treatment of complement-related diseases.
the development of a novel therapeutic approach to the treatment of diseases associated with uncontrolled complement activation.
a new strategy for the treatment of human diseases in which complement is activated inappropriately.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results presented here are a proof-of-principle that complement regulation can be targeted by the single-chain Ab-mediated delivery of a soluble complement regulator.
the use of single chain antibody fragments (scFv) to deliver complement regulatory molecules to RBCs in vivo is feasible.

the use of a single-chain Ab as a targeting vehicle for the delivery of a complement regulatory protein to a defined cell population can effectively and selectively inhibit complement activation in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the complement system can be targeted by a single-chain Ab, which is capable of delivering a complement regulatory protein to a defined cell population, thereby protecting this cell type from complement attack while leaving the rest of the complement system unaltered.
we have developed a novel strategy to deliver complement regulatory molecules to RBCs.
we have shown that the complement system can be regulated in a site-specific fashion using recombinant proteins targeted to a defined cell population.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we were able to show that the targeting of a recombinant complement regulatory protein (Crry, which protects RBCs from complement-mediated lysis) to the surface of RBCs can prolong their in vivo survival.
it is possible to target complement regulatory proteins to specific cell types, which could potentially be used in a clinical setting to treat diseases where the complement system plays a major role.
the complement inhibitory capacity can be restricted to a defined cell population by the use of a single-chain Ab targeting the cell surface and delivering complement regulatory proteins.
